newsitem.title: ROMANIA: Bucharest mayor likely Romania prime minister.
newsitem.headline: Bucharest mayor likely Romania prime minister.

text.p: The popular mayor of Bucharest was designated as Romania's future prime minister on Tuesday two days after reformist Emil Constantinescu won presidential elections, ousting former communists.

Victor Ciorbea was named by the Peasant Party (PNTCD), mainstay of the president-elect's Democratic Convention (CDR) group, to head the country's first coalition government not led by ex-communists since 1989.
Constantinescu, who turned 57 on Tuesday, later endorsed the nomination at a CDR meeting. He will be sworn in as president next week.

"We younger members of the party must not disappoint the historic figures who sacrificed a large part of their lives in communist prisons," Ciorbea, a lawyer and no-nonsense labour leader, said in an acceptance speech.
"After half a century we can say that communist structures have ceased to exist. Their place has been taken by democratic institutions."
The Peasant Party, created 75 years ago and affiliated to Europe's Christian Democrats, bore the brunt of Communist repression, with only a few of its current leaders surviving long prison terms.

Constantinescu ousted incumbent Ion Iliescu, a former communist who had led the country since 1989, in elections on Sunday. He has promised faster market reforms to improve some of eastern Europe's lowest living standards by blending tighter financial measures with increased pensions and benefits.

At 42, Ciorbea will be Romania's youngest prime minister. He earned a reputation as a tough negotiator in labour disputes against post-communist governments and became Bucharest mayor last June as the CDR standardbearer, thrashing Iliescu's handpicked candidate, former tennis star Ilie Nastase.
The CDR's victories then in town halls throughout the country were the first step in dethroning ex-communists.

It threw Iliescu's leftists out of government in this month's general elections and crowned that with Constantinescu's victory last weekend. Final results released on Tuesday gave him 54.4 percent to Iliescu's 45.6 percent.

Since taking over as Bucharest mayor Ciorbea has embarked on an ambitious programme of cleaning up the capital, providing housing for young couples and free public transport for pensioners and students.
In his acceptance speech, he pledged to implement Constantinescu's campaign pledges to cut taxes and improve social benefits, tempered by tough financial discipline.

The CDR is to govern in a coalition with the Social Democrats, led by former prime minister Petre Roman, earmarked for the post of chairman of the Senate -- the number two position after the president.
A deal struck by the two sides ahead of Constantinescu's election agreed to combine their campaign platforms but did not distribute cabinet posts. Commissions are to meet this week to allocate jobs.
The new government will apparently face even more economic difficulties than had been anticipated.
Outgoing Finance Minister Florin Georgescu announced revised higher figures for the 1996 budget deficit and inflation and blamed extra expenditure in an election year.
"Neither the deficit nor the budget itself is created by an individual but by a society with demands," Georgescu told reporters. "We gave in to pressure from social groups to index salaries."
